wiki_excerpt:
Inferno (Italian: [iɱˈfɛrno]; Italian for 'Hell') is the first part of the Italian writer Dante Alighieri's 14th-century narrative poem the Divine Comedy, followed by Purgatorio and Paradiso. The Inferno describes the journey of a fictionalised version of Dante himself through Hell, guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil. In the poem, Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment located within the Earth; it is the "realm [...] of those who have rejected spiritual values by yielding to bestial appetites or violence, or by perverting their human intellect to fraud or malice against their fellowmen". As an allegory, the Divine Comedy represents the journey of the soul toward God, with the Inferno describing the recognition and rejection of sin.


Composition and publication
Though definitive dates have not been established, Dante had most likely begun work on the Comedy around 1306; some modern scholars argue that Inferno's composition began as late as 1313, while early commentators proposed start dates prior to 1302. Dante was exiled from Florence in 1302 after his political faction, the pro-empire White Guelphs, were defeated by the pro-Papal Black Guelphs. Largely removed from politics and other scholarship, Dante spent nearly all of the last fifteen years of his life focused on the Comedy. "Many, but not all", scholars agree that Inferno was begun in 1306–1307 and completed in 1309–1310, though revisions likely continued for many years afterwards. Giovanni Boccaccio and some other early commentators argued that Dante composed the first seven cantos prior to his exile from Florence.
While the complete Comedy was likely not published until after Dante's death in 1321, Inferno circulated in fragments and excerpts for years prior. The earliest citations of the Inferno were written as early as 1315. The scholar Giorgio Petrocchi argues that Dante finished revising both Inferno and Purgatorio by 1317; both were likely fully drafted by 1313. However, other evidence suggests that Dante only began work on the poem much later; in particular, Dante's references to the Avignon Papacy and Clement V's death in 1314 have led some scholars to argue that Dante did not begin work on the poem until 1313. Others, such as Petrocchi, argue that these passages were small insertions during Dante's revisions—Dante makes sparse references to events after 1306, and Clement's death is the only event referenced in the Inferno to occur past 1310.


Prelude to Hell


Canto I

The poem begins on the night of Maundy Thursday on March 24 (or April 7), 1300, shortly before the dawn of Good Friday. grok_lead: The Inferno is the first canticle of Dante Alighieri's epic poem The Divine Comedy, composed primarily between 1306 and 1308, in which the author portrays his own allegorical pilgrimage through the infernal realms as a means to spiritual enlightenment. Written in the Tuscan vernacular rather than Latin, the work comprises 34 cantos structured around nine descending concentric circles of Hell, each punishing specific categories of sin through the principle of contrapasso, whereby the torment mirrors the fault committed in life. Guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil, Dante encounters historical and mythological figures suffering eternal damnation, blending classical paganism with Christian theology to critique moral failings, political corruption, and ecclesiastical abuses prevalent in medieval Florence and beyond. Employing the innovative terza rima rhyme scheme âinterlocking triplets of linesâthe Inferno not only revolutionized poetic form but also established the Italian vernacular as a vehicle for profound philosophical and theological discourse, profoundly influencing subsequent Western literature and conceptions of the afterlife. Its vivid depictions of retribution, from the lustful buffeted by tempests to traitors encased in ice, underscore a causal realism in divine justice, where empirical observation of human vice informs an unyielding first-principles framework for cosmic order.
